Hi Alice — jumping in with the technical answers + recommended patterns. I'll keep each item short and include a couple of small code snippets in the SDK style. See attached quickstart for auth examples.

1) Chat vs completions- Use chat for multi-turn stateful flows: it's optimized for message history, system roles, and function/tool calling. Completions are fine for single-shot generation but lose some convenience for structured tool calling. Cost/latency: chat models often have similar per-token pricing; difference comes from prompt size (chat message headers). For RAG + multi-turn we recommend chat + prefixing system prompt + truncated convo windows.

2) Tokenization & max_tokens- max_tokens is applied in token units (post-tokenization). Important notes:
  - When you set max_tokens on the server, it's the maximum number of tokens the model will generate, not count input tokens. Total token usage = input_tokens + output_tokens.
  - For long RAG contexts, we recommend: 1) limit upstream embedding results to top-N and truncate each doc to a fixed token budget, 2) use prefix/KV caching for repeated context, and 3) set a safe generation cap (e.g., 256-512) and enforce a request-side check for prompt length to avoid hitting model context limits.

SDK snippet (Python-like):
client.chat.create(model="redwood-chat-1", messages=[{"role":"system","content":"You are a support assistant."}, {"role":"user","content":"<user prompt + RAG docs truncated>"}], max_tokens=512)

3) Structured output & stop sequences- Best path for deterministic JSON: function/schema-based structured output (function calling) where the model returns a typed object. If you must use free-text JSON, stop sequences can help but are brittle (model can still emit extra content). Function/schema-based approach is recommended for production. Regarding streaming: when streaming structured output, you will receive partial fragments that you should buffer and parse only after the final delta (an "end_of_output" event) — Redwood's streaming protocol includes a finalization event to indicate complete object.

4) Streaming semantics and post-processing- Streaming is safe for UI responsiveness. For post-processing (rerankers, downstream pipelines), rely on the finalization signal before running deterministic pipelines. Caveats: partial token glitches can occur if you parse mid-stream; also function calls may be emitted as a single final object or as structured deltas depending on the model. We recommend: 1) stream to the UI for UX, 2) buffer the final response on the server for any downstream deterministic jobs, 3) use checksums or message ids to deduplicate.

5) Embeddings -> search -> rerank- Typical flow: 1) compute query embedding, 2) nearest-neighbors search (top-K), 3) prepare RAG prompt with the top-K docs (truncate to token budget), 4) call chat model to generate candidate responses, optionally 5) call a lightweight reranker (cheaper) to rescore top N candidates or perform a single-pass rerank using the chat model with a guided prompt. Trade-offs: single-pass rerank with a chat model is simple but more expensive; a dedicated reranker model (smaller) can be cost-effective if you need to rescore many candidates.

Attachment: redwood-sdk-quickstart.pdf — contains the auth examples (API key vs short-lived token exchange), SDK examples for chat/streaming, and sample reranker flow.

If helpful, I can paste a short runnable example for function calling + streaming during the call.
